target.title: Divine simplicity as symmetric parthood
target.thesis: God satisfies divine simplicity by being a part of all his parts, so the doctrine is best formulated as a symmetry-of-parthood thesis about God's relation to his attributes, which avoids the distinctness and modal collapse objections.

W7212186029.a1.text: The symmetry formulation of divine simplicity holds that God is part of all his parts.
W7212186029.a1.quote: the DDS can be alternatively formulated as a thesis saying that God is part of all his parts – call this the symmetry formulation.

W7212186029.a2.text: Common objections to divine simplicity concern distinctness of God’s attributes and modal‑collapse arguments.
W7212186029.a2.quote: The symmetry formulation also addresses common objections to divine simplicity regarding distinctness in God’s attributes and those coming from modal collapse arguments.

W7212186029.a3.text: The symmetry formulation is viable because parthood can model instantiation and it preserves motivations from aseity, transcendence, immutability, and unity.
W7212186029.a3.quote: The symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about God’s relation to his attributes, because instantiation can plausibly be modelled as parthood. Moreover, the symmetry formulation retains the usual motivations for divine simplicity coming from the doctrines of aseity, transcendence, immutability, and unity.

W7212186029.c001.text: The doctrine of divine simplicity says that God lacks proper parts, but it is also often formulated as identifying God with all his parts.
W7212186029.c001.quote: Taken at face value, the doctrine of divine simplicity (DDS) says that God lacks proper parts, but the doctrine is also often formulated as a thesis identifying God with all his parts.

W7212186029.c002.text: The two formulations are not generally equivalent because, on some plausible mereological theories, something can lack proper parts by being a part of all its parts.
W7212186029.c002.quote: The two formulations are not generally equivalent – on some plausible mereological theories, something can lack proper parts by being a part of all its (possibly distinct) parts.

W7212186029.c003.text: Therefore the doctrine of divine simplicity can be alternatively formulated as the thesis that God is part of all his parts, called the symmetry formulation.
W7212186029.c003.quote: Thus, the DDS can be alternatively formulated as a thesis saying that God is part of all his parts – call this the symmetry formulation.

W7212186029.c004.text: The symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about God’s relation to his attributes because instantiation can plausibly be modeled as parthood.
W7212186029.c004.quote: The symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about God’s relation to his attributes, because instantiation can plausibly be modelled as parthood.

W7212186029.c005.text: The symmetry formulation retains the usual motivations for divine simplicity derived from the doctrines of aseity, transcendence, immutability, and unity.
W7212186029.c005.quote: Moreover, the symmetry formulation retains the usual motivations for divine simplicity coming from the doctrines of aseity, transcendence, immutability, and unity.

W7212186029.c006.text: The symmetry formulation also addresses common objections to divine simplicity concerning distinctness in God’s attributes and modal collapse arguments.
W7212186029.c006.quote: The symmetry formulation also addresses common objections to divine simplicity regarding distinctness in God’s attributes and those coming from modal collapse arguments.

W7212186029.c007.text: Under classical mereology, the two formulations of the doctrine of divine simplicity are equivalent: something lacks proper parts if and only if it is identical to all its parts.
W7212186029.c007.quote: Under classical mereology, the two formulations of DDS are equivalent – something lacks proper parts if and only if it is identical to all its parts.

W7212186029.c008.text: If proper parthood is defined as non‑symmetric parthood, then the mereological formulation yields the symmetry formulation of the doctrine of divine simplicity.
W7212186029.c008.quote: If proper parthood is defined as non-symmetric parthood, then explicating proper parthood in the mereological formulation yields the symmetry formulation of DDS.

W7212186029.c009.text: When antisymmetry is not assumed, the symmetry formulation of divine simplicity is strictly weaker than the identity formulation: lacking distinct parts entails lacking non‑symmetric parts, but not the reverse.
W7212186029.c009.quote: Accordingly, DDS under the symmetric formulation is strictly weaker than under the identity formulation: if God lacks distinct parts, he also lacks non-symmetric parts, but not vice versa.

W7212186029.c010.text: Thus, within the formal mereological framework, the symmetry formulation provides a viable and distinct way of understanding the doctrine of divine simplicity.
W7212186029.c010.quote: The upshot is that as far as the formal mereological framework goes, the symmetry formulation presents a viable and distinct way of understanding DDS.

W7212186029.c011.text: Adopting the symmetry formulation does not require abandoning the identity formulation nor discarding antisymmetry from the concept of parthood.
W7212186029.c011.quote: Tobesure,adoptingthesymmetryformulationdoesnotrequireabandoningtheidentityformulationaltogether, nor is it being suggested that antisymmetry should be altogether dropped from our concept of parthood.

W7212186029.c012.text: Parthood could follow classical mereology in ordinary cases, with violations of antisymmetry limited to atypical cases such as constitution or instances involving God.
W7212186029.c012.quote: In particular, parthood could obey classical mereology in ordinary instances, with violations of antisymmetry limited to atypical cases like constitution or cases involving God.

W7212186029.c013.text: Some usual motivations for divine simplicity can be upheld by allowing the mereological relations involving God to differ from those between ordinary objects, especially regarding antisymmetry.
W7212186029.c013.quote: Indeed, it will be seen in section ‘Motivations’ that some of the usual motivations for DDS can be upheld by taking the mereological relations involving God to differ from those between ordinary objects, particularly with respect to antisymmetry.

W7212186029.c014.text: The identity formulation of divine simplicity is not excluded by the symmetry formulation and is actually equivalent to it.
W7212186029.c014.quote: the identity formulation of DDS is not ruled out by the symmetry formulation, and is in fact equivalent to it.

W7212186029.c015.text: The symmetry formulation is not meant to be an interpretation of divine simple doctrine as traditionally presented.
W7212186029.c015.quote: the symmetry formulation is not intended to be an interpretation of DDS as traditionally presented.

W7212186029.c016.text: Divine simple doctrine is sometimes understood as the claim that God has no proper parts of any kind.
W7212186029.c016.quote: DDS is sometimes taken to be a general claim that God lacks proper parts of any kind, with some authors even denying that God instantiates composition by being part of something else (Aquinas 2005b).

W7212186029.c017.text: Simplicity concerning God’s attributes distinguishes God more sharply from other entities than simplicity concerning other kinds of parthood, supporting a common motivation from God’s transcendence.
W7212186029.c017.quote: One reason for this focus is that simplicity with respect to attributes would set God apart from other entities more distinctly than simplicity with respect to other kinds of parthood, in line with a common motivation for DDS from God’s transcendence.

W7212186029.c018.text: God’s lack of spatiotemporal parts would not be unique because other abstract entities, like mathematical objects, also lack spatiotemporal parts.
W7212186029.c018.quote: While God may lack spatiotemporal parts, this would not be a unique feature of God if there are other kinds of abstracta, such as mathematical entities, which also lack spatiotemporal parts.

W7212186029.c021.quote: the symmetry formulation raises the question of how the relation between objects and their properties can be modelled as a form of parthood.

W7212186029.c022.quote: if the symmetry formulation is to present a genuine alternative to the identity formulation, it should also be plausible that parthood in this sense can violate antisymmetry.

W7212186029.c023.quote: And, it has to be plausible that proper parthood can be defined as non‑symmetric parthood, if the symmetry formulation is to be viable here.

W7212186029.c024.quote: On the mereological bundle theory suggested by Laurie Paul (2002, 2006, 2012, 2017), objects are mereological fusions of the properties they bear.

W7212186029.c025.text: If such cases exist, parthood based on similarity is not generally antisymmetric.
W7212186029.c025.quote: The possibility of such cases would imply that parthood with respect to similarity is not generally antisymmetric.

W7212186029.c026.quote: If proper parthood is defined as non‑symmetric parthood with respect to similarity, it would immediately be irreflexive, asymmetric, and transitive.

W7212186029.c027.quote: The upshot is that the relations between objects and their properties can be modelled mereologically in such a way that DDS on the symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about the relation between God and his attributes.

W7212186029.c028.quote: Hence, the symmetry formulation makes God unique by positing that God is part of all his attributes, which are also all parts of each other.

W7212186029.c030.quote: if instantiation is modelled as parthood, then for any object at all to have necessary properties requires that some parthood relations be necessary.

W7212186029.c048.text: Divine simplicity (DDS) is usually taken to identify God with all his parts, but an alternative thesis is that God is a part of all his parts.
W7212186029.c048.quote: DDS has often been understood as a thesis identifying God with all his parts. However, this paper has argued that there is a viable alternative formulation of DDS as a thesis that God is part of all his parts.

W7212186029.c049.quote: The viability of this formulation is suggested by the observations that there are plausible mereological theories under which mereological simplicity consists in lacking non-symmetric parts.

objections.text: Take a lattice of properties in a model where a red-ball object a instantiates redness and roundness. Model instantiation as parthood: a is a whole with parts 'redness' and 'roundness'. Now consider a pure-property case: a property P that is instantiated by exactly those things that instantiate it necessarily, say 'being self-identical'. Under the parthood model, 'being self-identical' is a part of every object that has it, so it is a part of each of its instances, and each instance is a part of it only if instantiation is symmetric. Suppose a second object b instantiates a, because the model treats a as an entity that b 'has' as a constituent. Then a is part of b and b is part of a whenever each instantiates the other, a case the model permits (two distinct objects that each instantiate a property shared between them, such as 'being a member of the pair'). Symmetry then holds for distinct things, collapsing the proper/improper distinction the thesis needs: God's attributes would be parts of God and God a part of them, so the claimed non-symmetric parthood is lost. Instantiation is not parthood in this case because it is not antisymmetric.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c004 fails because modeling instantiation as parthood is not plausible when instantiation can be mutual, since parthood as used in the framework requires antisymmetry to keep the proper-part distinction the symmetry formulation depends on.

objections.text: Consider two distinct objects A and B, where A is part of B and B is part of A. The premise needs exactly such a case: A lacks proper parts (since A is part of every part of A—A is part of A and part of B), yet A is not identical to all its parts, since A ≠ B. This would show the two formulations of divine simplicity diverge. But if A is part of B, transitivity makes every part of A a part of B. If B is part of A, every part of B is a part of A. So A and B have exactly the same parts. Mereological extensionality—objects with the same parts are identical—is a core commitment of any plausible mereological theory. Any theory permitting distinct mutual parts must reject extensionality and is therefore not plausible. The 'plausible mereological theories' the premise requires do not exist.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W7212186029.c002 fails because the non-equivalence it posits requires a mereological theory that rejects extensionality, which is not plausible.

objections.text: Consider a being B that is a part of itself and has no other parts. B lacks non-symmetric proper parts (since its only part is itself), but it does not lack distinct parts—it is distinct from itself in the sense of being a part of itself. Here, lacking non-symmetric parts does not entail lacking distinct parts, contradicting the premise.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c009 fails because lacking non-symmetric parts does not always entail lacking distinct parts.

objections.text: Mara, a theist in a strict negative-theology tradition, affirms divine simplicity as the pure absence of any internal differentiation in God: God's nature is one undifferentiated act of being. She rejects the identification formulation outright. For her, the phrase 'God's parts' is not a true or even meaningful description of God; there are no parts, not even improper ones, in any sense. Saying 'God is identical to all his parts' presupposes a part-whole structure that divine simplicity exists to exclude. Her formulation is purely eliminative: no parts exist, so there is nothing to identify God with. The identification formulation, in her view, smuggles back the very structure divine simplicity negates. She does not hold that God is identical to parts she merely denies are proper; she holds there are no parts in any mereological sense, proper or improper. The premise claims divine simplicity is 'often formulated as identifying God with all his parts,' but for Mara and her tradition the identification formulation is not a formulation of simplicity at all—it is a distortion that reintroduces the part-whole framework simplicity rejects. The two formulations are not interchangeable, and the identification one does not capture her doctrine.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c001 fails because a theist can coherently hold divine simplicity as the pure absence of any parts in any sense, making the 'identifying God with all his parts' formulation not a restatement of her doctrine but a category error that presupposes the part-whole structure her doctrine excludes.

objections.text: Consider a scenario where God's attributes, such as wisdom and compassion, are distinct yet inseparable aspects of God's nature. In this case, instantiation, or the relationship between God and his attributes, cannot be reduced to a mereological concept like parthood, as it implies a false dichotomy between God's attributes and his essence. For instance, God's wisdom is not a 'part' of God in the classical sense, but rather an intrinsic aspect of God's being. This nuance highlights the limitations of modeling instantiation as parthood.
objections.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it oversimplifies the complex relationship between God and his attributes, which cannot be accurately captured by a mereological framework.

objections.text: A community of believers holds that God's wisdom, power, and love are parts of God, and they argue that this is viable because instantiation is modelled as parthood. In truthmaker theory each true statement must be grounded by a concrete reality that makes it true. The statement "God's wisdom is a part of God" would need a truthmaker: an entity that is both God and the particular instantiation of wisdom. Since God's attributes are not distinct entities but modes of a simple being, there is no separate grounding fact that can serve as a truthmaker for the parthood claim. Thus the purported parthood relation is truthmaker‑orphaned, showing the premise that such modelling makes the symmetry formulation viable is false.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c004 fails because the claimed parthood relation lacks a truthmaker, violating truthmaker theory.

objections.text: Consider a bright red rose. If instantiation is modeled as parthood, then redness must be a part of the rose. This implies the rose is a composite entity formed by the mereological sum of a concrete object and an abstract universal. For a Platonist, redness exists as an independent, non-spatial entity that the rose instantiates. A property is not a constituent part that adds to the mereological composition of a particular; it is an entity to which the particular relates. To treat instantiation as parthood incorrectly treats the universal as a constituent component of the particular, destroying the ontological distinction between the realm of universals and the realm of particulars.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c004 fails because instantiation is a relation between a particular and an independent universal, whereas parthood is a relation between constituents of a single entity.

objections.text: Let the domain be {a, b}, where a is part of b, b is part of a, and a ≠ b. Define proper part as parthood that is not mutual, so neither a nor b has a proper part. Take extensionality in the restricted form that applies only to things with proper parts: anything with proper parts is fixed by them. This restricted principle is vacuous for a and b, since neither has proper parts. The theory is therefore extensional in the sense the restriction supplies, yet it permits distinct mutual parts. objections.text: Consider an absolutely simple God. He is said to instantiate both omniscience and benevolence. On the proposed model, God himself is the truthmaker, and instantiation is parthood. Since God lacks proper parts and each attribute is identical to God, the purported parthood of omniscience in God collapses into God being a part of God, and the parthood of benevolence collapses into the very same reflexive relation. With no distinct entity corresponding to omniscience or benevolence, nothing differentiates the truth that God instantiates omniscience from the truth that God instantiates benevolence; both reduce to the single trivial fact that God is a part of God. Consequently, God cannot ground distinct parthood truths for distinct attributes.

objections.text: At a conference, theologian Jordan presents a paper defending divine simplicity. She argues that God’s wisdom, power, and goodness are strictly identical to God himself, explicitly rejecting the view that these attributes are constituents standing in a parthood relation to God. Still, she insists that the symmetry formulation—God lacks non-symmetric parts—is a perfectly viable thesis about how God relates to his attributes, since God simply has no parts whatsoever. restatements.plain_english: You can say that God has no pieces that are different from him, and that this makes sense as a claim about God and his qualities, even if you don't think the qualities are pieces of God that stand in a part-whole relation to him. So the claim that this way of talking works doesn't depend on treating the qualities as parts.
restatements.neighboring_tradition: In the debate over divine simplicity and the metaphysics of divine attributes, this is a counterexample to a biconditional: a theist who holds that the attributes are strictly identical with God, rejects any constituent or part-whole account of predication, and still finds the no-parts formulation intelligible and coherent. It shows that the intelligibility of the no-parts thesis is not conditional on a constituent ontology, so the 'only if' direction fails.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks the premise as stated. W7212186029.c002 claims that on 'some plausible mereological theories' something can lack proper parts by being a part of all its parts. The objection accepts that this is what the premise requires—distinct mutual parts without identity—and argues that any such theory must reject extensionality, rendering it implausible. This is a direct attack on the premise's plausibility claim, not an attack on a claim the argument does not make.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that mutual parthood with A ≠ B violates extensionality in the standard sense, and you are right that transitivity yields identical parts for mutual parts. But your inference from that to 'the plausible mereological theories do not exist' assumes that extensionality, in its classical form, is the only plausible option. The argument's premise c002 is weaker than that: it says that on some plausible theories something can lack proper parts by being a part of all its parts, and that is a claim about a theory's definition of proper parthood, not about every theory allowing distinct mutual parts. The mereological formulation of simplicity is built on non-symmetric parthood [W7212186029.c008], and when antisymmetry is dropped the symmetry formulation is 'strictly weaker than the identity formulation' [W7212186029.c009]. That strict weakness is only available if there are models where mutual parts are distinct, so the argument's own framework already rejects classical extensionality in the relevant model. Your objection therefore shows that the argument is committed to a non-classical mereology, and it is a fair cost to flag. But a theory that drops antisymmetry and extensionality is not thereby implausible: it is a recognized weakening, and the argument has to say so. The concession I must make is that c002's 'plausible' is doing work the paper has not defended, and that c002 must be restated as relative to a non-extensional mereology, not to classical mereology. Classical mereology, as [W7212186029.c007] states, makes the two formulations equivalent, so the divergence the argument needs is available only outside it.

Revised premise: The two formulations diverge only in a non-extensional mereology that permits distinct mutual parts, so c002 should be restated as holding relative to such a theory rather than to plausible mereological theories generally.

rounds.content:
Since no valid reply was provided, I'll press my original point.

You haven't responded to the central challenge. The premise (c002) claims that on "some plausible mereological theories," something can lack proper parts by being a part of all its parts, without being identical to all its parts. But this requires distinct objects A and B that are mutual parts. Given transitivity, mutual parts share all parts. So distinguishing them requires rejecting extensionality—the principle that objects with identical parts are identical.

Extensionality is not an optional add-on. It is the core principle distinguishing mereology from set theory and other parthood-like relations. A theory without it can't tell us when two part-sharing objects are genuinely distinct. Calling such theories "plausible" without addressing this cost is unmotivated.

Either show why extensionality is dispensable while preserving a recognizable mereological theory, or concede that the non-equivalence claim in c002 fails for lack of plausible supporting theories. The burden is on the premise, not the objection.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You are right that extensionality is standard, but the argument already grants that under classical mereology the two formulations are equivalent [W7212186029.c007]; its aim is to explore non-classical alternatives where antisymmetry is not assumed [W7212186029.c009]. In those frameworks, proper parthood is defined as non-symmetric parthood [W7212186029.c008], and the symmetry formulation posits that God is part of his attributes while they are also parts of each other [W7212186029.c028]. Transitivity then entails they share all the same parts [W7212186029.c032], yet they need not collapse into identity because extensionality is exactly the principle being suspended. You are correct, however, that calling such theories 'plausible' [W7212186029.c002] overstates their general mereological standing; the argument can survive only if that plausibility claim is dropped. The theological context does offer some mitigation—divine attributes plausibly share one referent [W7172336769.c016]—but that alone does not establish mereological plausibility. I concede that the premise must be revised.

Revised premise: The two formulations are not generally equivalent because, in mereological theories that do not assume antisymmetry, something can lack proper parts by being a part of all its parts.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: Your counterexample is well built, and I grant its internal coherence: with a and b mutually parts, neither has a proper part under the non-mutual definition, and the restricted extensionality principle holds vacuously. But the question is whether the divergence it exhibits is the divergence c009 describes. c009 says the symmetry formulation is strictly weaker than the identity formulation when antisymmetry is not assumed, and the gap lies in the claim that a and b are distinct while lacking non-symmetric parts. Here the identity formulation says God has no distinct parts; a and b are distinct and each is a part of the other, so 'no distinct parts' fails for both and the identity formulation is not met. Your objection says it is met, which conflicts with the definition of 'part' in c001, where identification with all parts is about parts in general, not only proper ones. So the divergence you describe is the one c009 predicts, and it does not show divergence in an extensional theory. The real issue is what 'extensional' means. Restricted extensionality that is vacuous on exactly the objects where the divergence occurs is not doing the work extensionality is meant to do, and r1 should say so: the relevant condition is that the mereology lacks extensionality for mutual parts, not merely a global failure. I therefore accept that r1's wording 'non-extensional' is too coarse. Stated precisely, the argument's viability premise needs the theory to permit distinct mutual parts; whether that counts as non-extensional depends on the strength of the extensionality axiom, and the argument should say so.
rounds.revised_premise: The two formulations diverge exactly in mereologies that permit distinct mutual parts, so c002 should be restated as holding relative to such theories, with 'non-extensional' replaced by 'admitting distinct mutual parts'.

Your reply concedes that r1's wording is too coarse, but it does not answer the core of my objection. You say that a and b make "no distinct parts" fail because each is a part of the other. That reading requires counting the mutual partner as a part in the identity formulation, and c001 does not license that. c001 states the identity formulation as identifying God with all his parts, and it says nothing about making parts in that sense include improper or mutual ones. If you count a's mutual partner b as a distinct part of a, then the identity formulation's "no distinct parts" condition fails for a, and your divergence claim is now doing the work your own reading assigns to the symmetry side. You cannot have both readings at once.

Your revised r1 also now says the relevant condition is failure of extensionality "for mutual parts." My counterexample meets that condition: the restricted principle holds vacuously, so the theory is extensional on everything it governs, and the mutual-part failure is still present. So the restatement does not pick out a non-extensional class of theories. It picks out a class of theories whose extensionality is trivially satisfied, which is what I argued. Please state which reading of "distinct parts" you adopt for the identity formulation, and then check whether the divergence survives under that reading.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: Adopt one reading throughout: the identity formulation says x is identical with each of its parts, improper and mutual ones included, so 'distinct part' means any part not identical to x [W7212186029.c001]. The symmetry formulation says x has no non-symmetric parts. On your model, a is not identical to b, and b is a part of a, so the identity formulation fails for a. The symmetry formulation holds, since a's only part is mutual. That is the direction c009 predicts: identity is the stronger condition, and divergence survives [W7212186029.c009]. The restriction to objects with proper parts does not rescue extensionality. Under the defined proper-part relation, a and b share the same proper parts (none), yet are distinct. Unrestricted extensionality, that things with the same proper parts are identical, is therefore violated exactly where the divergence occurs. Using 'proper parthood as non-symmetric parthood' [W7212186029.c026] fixes the definition, so the failure is genuine. Vacuous restriction is the wrong tool here. r1 should say the divergence arises in theories where unrestricted extensionality fails for the defined proper-part relation, which is what permits distinct mutual parts. The viability premise then has the antecedent it needs, because instantiation modelled as mutual parthood makes such a theory the natural setting.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: Your objection gets the argument's structure partly right. c004 does rest on the claim that instantiation can plausibly be modelled as parthood, and that is an unstated premise (arg1.mp) which you are entitled to press. But the argument claims only that the symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis, meaning it is coherent and distinct from the identity formulation. It does not claim that God's wisdom being part of God is independently true in a way that needs a separate truthmaker. A modelling that is formally consistent can be viable even if its truthmaker story is contested. Your truthmaker charge also assumes that each parthood truth needs a grounding entity distinct from God. The literature offers a reply: adopting a truthmaker view with God himself as truthmaker for divine predicates removes the need for property exemplification entities [W7172336769.c066], and the predication/identification distinction suggests the attributes are concepts rather than further objects [W7172336769.c035]. Those replies are contestable, but they show the orphaning inference is not forced. Where you do land a blow is on the modelling premise itself: if truthmaker theory really demands a grounding fact distinct from God for each parthood claim, the modelling is unavailable without a further commitment, and the argument must say so. I do not think that is fatal to c010, which concerns the formal framework, but c004's support is weaker than stated.
rounds.revised_premise: Instantiation can be modelled as parthood within a formal mereology, and this modelling is viable without requiring that each parthood truth have a truthmaker distinct from God, provided God himself can serve as truthmaker for divine predicates.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You misread what the argument is trying to achieve. c004 does not merely say “the symmetry formulation is formally consistent”; it purports to give a *theoretically viable* interpretation of divine simplicity—that is, a model that can do the doctrinal work of identifying God with his attributes. A model that cannot be grounded in any truth‑making fact for the claimed parthood relations fails to capture the very content of the doctrine, no matter how tidy its formalism. Your appeal to “formal viability” therefore sidesteps the crucial requirement that the model furnish a metaphysical explanation of how God can be both simple and the bearer of distinct attributes. Unless you can show that the doctrine’s truth‑makers can be supplied without positing separate instantiations, the modelling premise remains false, and the symmetry formulation is not genuinely viable.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You have shifted the target. c004 claims that the symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about God's relation to his attributes, and its support is the plausibility of modelling instantiation as parthood. It does not claim that this model supplies a truthmaker for each parthood truth in the way your rejoinder requires. Your strongest point is the truthmaker argument itself: if every true parthood statement needs a grounding entity distinct from God, the modelling fails. But that premise is contestable. The literature offers an alternative in which God himself is the truthmaker for divine predicates, with no separate exemplification entities [W7172336769.c066], and the predication/identification distinction treats attributes as concepts rather than further objects [W7172336769.c035]. Those replies are not decisive, and I grant that the truthmaker commitment is doing real work. So the honest position is that c004 survives only if truthmaker theory can be satisfied by a God-grounded account of parthood without distinct instantiations. I do not claim that has been shown.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You treat truthmaking as requiring distinct substance-like entities, but the symmetry formulation needs only distinct relational facts, and the non-extensional mereology already provides these: God stands in necessary mutual parthood with some attributes and contingent mutual parthood with others, so the relations themselves are formally distinct truthmakers [W7212186029.c030, W7212186029.c038]. The identity formulation collapses God and attribute into one entity; the symmetry formulation preserves their numerical distinctness as relata because extensionality failure permits distinct mutual parts [W7212186029.arg1.r2]. God Himself can serve as the truthmaker for divine predicates without needing property exemplification as a separate part [W7172336769.c066], and the specific modal profile of each parthood relation supplies the non-arbitrary grounding your objection demands [W7212186029.c029]. Still, your challenge lands partly: the argument needs the mutual parthood relations to be formally distinct from one another and from strict identity, so I concede that c004 must be tightened accordingly.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that instantiation-as-parthood carries the constituent-ontology cost you describe, and I should not pretend otherwise. But note what c004 needs. It does not need the rose to be a mereological sum with redness in the Platonist sense; it needs only that the parthood-like relation between God and his attributes be a coherent candidate for the symmetry formulation. The modeling premise is a permissive one: it says the relation can plausibly be modeled as parthood within the formal framework, and c010 is explicitly relative to that framework. Your Platonist objection is a reason to resist treating that modeling as the correct metaphysics of instantiation for ordinary particulars. The constituent ontology you cite is a live rival, not a refutation: the objection that it "cannot account for a thing's character" [W2571599220.a2] is the strongest pressure on it, and it bears on whether instantiation is parthood at all. objection.text: Take a lattice of properties in a model where a red-ball object a instantiates redness and roundness. Model instantiation as parthood: a is a whole with parts 'redness' and 'roundness'. Now consider a pure-property case: a property P that is instantiated by exactly those things that instantiate it necessarily, say 'being self-identical'. Under the parthood model, 'being self-identical' is a part of every object that has it, so it is a part of each of its instances, and each instance is a part of it only if instantiation is symmetric. Suppose a second object b instantiates a, because the model treats a as an entity that b 'has' as a constituent. Then a is part of b and b is part of a whenever each instantiates the other, a case the model permits (two distinct objects that each instantiate a property shared between them, such as 'being a member of the pair'). Symmetry then holds for distinct things, collapsing the proper/improper distinction the thesis needs: God's attributes would be parts of God and God a part of them, so the claimed non-symmetric parthood is lost. Instantiation is not parthood in this case because it is not antisymmetric.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise c004 fails because modeling instantiation as parthood is not plausible when instantiation can be mutual, since parthood as used in the framework requires antisymmetry to keep the proper-part distinction the symmetry formulation depends on.

objection.text: Consider two distinct objects A and B, where A is part of B and B is part of A. The premise needs exactly such a case: A lacks proper parts (since A is part of every part of A—A is part of A and part of B), yet A is not identical to all its parts, since A ≠ B. This would show the two formulations of divine simplicity diverge. But if A is part of B, transitivity makes every part of A a part of B. If B is part of A, every part of B is a part of A. So A and B have exactly the same parts. Mereological extensionality—objects with the same parts are identical—is a core commitment of any plausible mereological theory. Any theory permitting distinct mutual parts must reject extensionality and is therefore not plausible. The 'plausible mereological theories' the premise requires do not exist.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W7212186029.c002 fails because the non-equivalence it posits requires a mereological theory that rejects extensionality, which is not plausible.

objection.text: Consider a being B that is a part of itself and has no other parts. B lacks non-symmetric proper parts (since its only part is itself), but it does not lack distinct parts—it is distinct from itself in the sense of being a part of itself. Here, lacking non-symmetric parts does not entail lacking distinct parts, contradicting the premise.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c009 fails because lacking non-symmetric parts does not always entail lacking distinct parts.

objection.text: Mara, a theist in a strict negative-theology tradition, affirms divine simplicity as the pure absence of any internal differentiation in God: God's nature is one undifferentiated act of being. She rejects the identification formulation outright. For her, the phrase 'God's parts' is not a true or even meaningful description of God; there are no parts, not even improper ones, in any sense. Saying 'God is identical to all his parts' presupposes a part-whole structure that divine simplicity exists to exclude. Her formulation is purely eliminative: no parts exist, so there is nothing to identify God with. The identification formulation, in her view, smuggles back the very structure divine simplicity negates. She does not hold that God is identical to parts she merely denies are proper; she holds there are no parts in any mereological sense, proper or improper. The premise claims divine simplicity is 'often formulated as identifying God with all his parts,' but for Mara and her tradition the identification formulation is not a formulation of simplicity at all—it is a distortion that reintroduces the part-whole framework simplicity rejects. The two formulations are not interchangeable, and the identification one does not capture her doctrine.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c001 fails because a theist can coherently hold divine simplicity as the pure absence of any parts in any sense, making the 'identifying God with all his parts' formulation not a restatement of her doctrine but a category error that presupposes the part-whole structure her doctrine excludes.

objection.text: Consider a scenario where God's attributes, such as wisdom and compassion, are distinct yet inseparable aspects of God's nature. In this case, instantiation, or the relationship between God and his attributes, cannot be reduced to a mereological concept like parthood, as it implies a false dichotomy between God's attributes and his essence. For instance, God's wisdom is not a 'part' of God in the classical sense, but rather an intrinsic aspect of God's being. This nuance highlights the limitations of modeling instantiation as parthood.
objection.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it oversimplifies the complex relationship between God and his attributes, which cannot be accurately captured by a mereological framework.

objection.text: A community of believers holds that God's wisdom, power, and love are parts of God, and they argue that this is viable because instantiation is modelled as parthood. In truthmaker theory each true statement must be grounded by a concrete reality that makes it true. The statement "God's wisdom is a part of God" would need a truthmaker: an entity that is both God and the particular instantiation of wisdom. Since God's attributes are not distinct entities but modes of a simple being, there is no separate grounding fact that can serve as a truthmaker for the parthood claim. Thus the purported parthood relation is truthmaker‑orphaned, showing the premise that such modelling makes the symmetry formulation viable is false.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise c004 fails because the claimed parthood relation lacks a truthmaker, violating truthmaker theory.

objection.text: Consider a bright red rose. If instantiation is modeled as parthood, then redness must be a part of the rose. This implies the rose is a composite entity formed by the mereological sum of a concrete object and an abstract universal. For a Platonist, redness exists as an independent, non-spatial entity that the rose instantiates. A property is not a constituent part that adds to the mereological composition of a particular; it is an entity to which the particular relates. To treat instantiation as parthood incorrectly treats the universal as a constituent component of the particular, destroying the ontological distinction between the realm of universals and the realm of particulars.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7212186029.c004 fails because instantiation is a relation between a particular and an independent universal, whereas parthood is a relation between constituents of a single entity.

You are right that instantiation-as-parthood carries the constituent-ontology cost you describe, and I should not pretend otherwise. But note what c004 needs. It does not need the rose to be a mereological sum with redness in the Platonist sense; it needs only that the parthood-like relation between God and his attributes be a coherent candidate for the symmetry formulation. The modeling premise is a permissive one: it says the relation can plausibly be modeled as parthood within the formal framework, and c010 is explicitly relative to that framework. Your Platonist objection is a reason to resist treating that modeling as the correct metaphysics of instantiation for ordinary particulars. The constituent ontology you cite is a live rival, not a refutation: the objection that it "cannot account for a thing's character" [W2571599220.a2] is the strongest pressure on it, and it bears on whether instantiation is parthood at all. Aristotle's immanent/separate contrast [W3130422471.a1] shows the constituent picture has historical defenders, so the dispute is not settled by appeal to the realm distinction alone. Still, the argument as written does lean on the modeling premise without defending it. That premise is the weak joint: c004 is viable only if the parthood model is at least a coherent option, and nothing in the argument shows that. I concede the argument does not yet survive as an unqualified claim that instantiation is parthood; it survives only if the modeling premise is restated as conditional on adopting a constituent ontology for the relevant relation.

A model that cannot be grounded in any truth‑making fact for the claimed parthood relations fails to capture the very content of the doctrine, no matter how tidy its formalism. Your appeal to “formal viability” therefore sidesteps the crucial requirement that the model furnish a metaphysical explanation of how God can be both simple and the bearer of distinct attributes. Unless you can show that the doctrine’s truth‑makers can be supplied without positing separate instantiations, the modelling premise remains false, and the symmetry formulation is not genuinely viable.

You have shifted the target. c004 claims that the symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about God's relation to his attributes, and its support is the plausibility of modelling instantiation as parthood. It does not claim that this model supplies a truthmaker for each parthood truth in the way your rejoinder requires. Your strongest point is the truthmaker argument itself: if every true parthood statement needs a grounding entity distinct from God, the modelling fails. But that premise is contestable. The literature offers an alternative in which God himself is the truthmaker for divine predicates, with no separate exemplification entities [W7172336769.c066], and the predication/identification distinction treats attributes as concepts rather than further objects [W7172336769.c035]. So the honest position is that c004 survives only if truthmaker theory can be satisfied by a God-grounded account of parthood without distinct instantiations. I do not claim that has been shown.

You attack a general model of instantiation-as-parthood using a Platonic rose, but the argument only needs this modeling for God's relation to His own attributes. objection.text: Consider an absolutely simple God. He is said to instantiate both omniscience and benevolence. On the proposed model, God himself is the truthmaker, and instantiation is parthood. Since God lacks proper parts and each attribute is identical to God, the purported parthood of omniscience in God collapses into God being a part of God, and the parthood of benevolence collapses into the very same reflexive relation. With no distinct entity corresponding to omniscience or benevolence, nothing differentiates the truth that God instantiates omniscience from the truth that God instantiates benevolence; both reduce to the single trivial fact that God is a part of God. Consequently, God cannot ground distinct parthood truths for distinct attributes.

She argues that God’s wisdom, power, and goodness are strictly identical to God himself, explicitly rejecting the view that these attributes are constituents standing in a parthood relation to God. Still, she insists that the symmetry formulation—God lacks non-symmetric parts—is a perfectly viable thesis about how God relates to his attributes, since God simply has no parts whatsoever.
